fetched_contents.text: Pitch characteristics of real-world infant-directed speech vary with pragmatic context, perceived adult gender, and infant gender Abstract Children’s everyday language environments can be full of rich and diverse input, especially adult speech. Prosodic modifications when adults speak to infants are observed cross-culturally and are believed to enhance infant learning and emotion. However, factors such as what and why adults are speaking as well as speaker gender can affect the prosody of adults’ speech. This study asks whether prosodic modifications to infant-directed speech depend on perceived adult speaker gender, assigned infant gender, and the perceived pragmatic function of an utterance. We examined 3,607 adult speech clips from daylong home audio recordings of 60 North American, English-speaking, 3- to 20-month-old infants (28 female). Adult speakers used significantly more imperatives and questions and sang more frequently to infants than other adults. While infant-directed speech tended to have greater mean pitch and pitch modulation than adult-directed speech overall, these patterns were modulated, sometimes in complex ways, by pragmatic function, perceived adult gender, and infant gender. For example, we found that female-sounding adult speakers exhibited greater IDS-ADS mean pitch differences than male-sounding adult speakers when providing information or engaging in conversational niceties. An additional example is that male-sounding adults used higher pitch when singing to male infants compared to female infants. These findings invite further research on how individual, demographic, and situational factors affect speech to infants and possibly infant learning. The study’s pragmatic context tags are added to an existing open dataset of infant- and adult-directed speech. Introduction Adults speak differently to infants than to other adults. This phenomenon is established across cultures [1–3]. Infant-directed speech (IDS) often differs from adult-directed speech (ADS) in having higher pitch, greater variation in intonation and other prosodic features [3–5], elongated vowels [6], shorter utterances [7], and simpler lexicons [8]. These differences are believed to have benefits for children’s attention to and acquisition of language [9–11]. The focus of the current study is on voice pitch across IDS and ADS registers. Although some speakers and some cultures manipulate IDS acoustics more than others, generally speaking, adults tend to use overall higher pitch [2] and more pitch modulations when speaking to infants compared to adults [3]. It has been theorized that higher pitch may help infants to match adult speech acoustics to their own, facilitating comparison between self-produced and caregiver-produced utterances [12]. Others have emphasized that greater pitch variability within an utterance may make it more attention-grabbing or help to highlight key words to facilitate infant language learning [13]. It is important to note that much of the research on acoustic differences between IDS and ADS is limited to speech samples produced in specific contexts, with most of the focus being on the speech that is intended to engage an infant’s interest and facilitate language–learning. Moreover, speech samples are often obtained through elicitation by a researcher. In contrast, infants often experience infant-directed speech that has a range of different goals, for example, that of soothing, rather than exciting, and of perhaps facilitating sleep or cessation of an activity, rather than engagement in conversation or with objects. In addition, the ways in which adults speak in real-world settings, such as in their homes while interacting with multiple family members and engaged in various day-to-day tasks and facing various stressors, have the potential to greatly alter the acoustic features of both ADS and IDS. Pragmatic contexts and acoustic characteristics Despite general trends differentiating IDS from ADS registers, there is also research indicating that pragmatics, or the functional use of speech, affects speech acoustics in ways that may modulate the IDS-ADS differences. For infant-directed speech, pragmatic contexts can include attention-bidding, approval, prohibition, soothing, and singing [14], among others. Prior work has demonstrated that pitch can vary across pragmatic contexts. For example, mothers are more likely to use lower pitch when soothing an infant [14] and higher pitch when trying to get an infant’s attention [14,15]. Research has also found that adults use greater pitch variability when arousing or entertaining infants, but less variable pitch when soothing infants [16,17]. When singing, parents tend to use a higher pitch [3,18,19]. Moreover, different pragmatic types of singing have different acoustic features: Trainor et al. found that infant play songs were rated to have greater pitch variability than infant lullabies [18]. Pitch differences are also associated with pragmatics (e.g., agreement, criticism, suggestion) in adult speech to other adults [20]. Effects of adult and infant gender on communication Another factor that can strongly influence adult voice acoustics is gender. Adult females generally have higher voice pitch compared to adult males [21,22] as well as other acoustic differences. These speaker gender differences in voice acoustics are in part attributable to anatomical differences between males and females in vocal folds and the vocal tracts associated with speech production [21,23]. In addition to anatomical differences, sociocultural factors contribute to differences in voice acoustics between males and females [21]. For example, a speaker’s emotional state, race, sex, and age can also affect acoustic variation [24] as well as social and cultural influences [25]. Introduction Speakers commonly consider their listeners when talking and adjust the characteristics of their speech accordingly (Bell, Reference Bell1984; Clark & Murphy, Reference Clark and Murphy1982). The concept of audience design applies to many different types of listeners, such as those who are hard-of-hearing, those who speak a different language, AI devices, and infants and children (Cohn et al., Reference Cohn, Segedin and Zellou2022; Lam & Kitamura, Reference Lam and Kitamura2012; Uther et al., Reference Uther, Knoll and Burnham2007). The register that adults use when interacting with infants is known as infant-directed speech (IDS). It is often characterised by having heightened pitch (perceived fundamental frequency, F0), slower rate, vowel space expansion/hyperarticulation, and longer vowel duration (Cooper & Aslin, Reference Cooper and Aslin1990; Cristia & Seidl, Reference Cristia and Seidl2014; Kuhl et al., Reference Kuhl, Andruski, Chistovich, Chistovich, Kozhevnikova, Ryskina, Stolyarova, Sundberg and Lacerda1997; but see Englund, Reference Englund2018). These features of IDS are well-documented, but an open question is to what extent features of IDS vary across communicative contexts for a parent and child. Like adults, infants do not experience language in a singular context. In day-to-day life, infants experience a variety of settings that alter the sounds, references, grammatical constructions, and lexical co-occurrences of a word. For example, “car” during story time can involve a narrative about an anthropomorphised car trying to win a race, whereas “car” on a road trip viewed among trucks, vans, and Sport Utility Vehicles (SUVs), can present opportunities to learn about categories (i.e., vehicles). However, the majority of studies examining IDS features have focused on a single type of interaction, spontaneous speech during play. A smaller number of studies have compared multiple contexts, usually two, such as read versus spontaneous speech (Cox et al., Reference Cox, Bergmann, Fowler, Keren-Portnoy, Roepstorff, Bryant and Fusaroli2022). Thus, we have little knowledge of the ways that parents adjust acoustic features of IDS when communicating across a range of different contexts with different goals. Indeed, parents talk to their infants in many different settings with various communicative goals throughout their everyday lives, yet most studies do not take this into account. The current study addresses whether parents display acoustic variation across different contexts when talking with their infants. Studying acoustic characteristics of IDS across multiple contexts tests the degree to which audience design is sensitive to the specific communicative needs of the situation and not just defined by the type of interlocutor. 2. Acoustic features of IDS Heightened fundamental frequency (F0), perceived as pitch, is one of the most salient features of IDS. Many studies have shown that mean pitch is typically raised in IDS relative to adult-directed speech (ADS) (Cooper & Aslin, Reference Cooper and Aslin1990; Kuhl et al., Reference Kuhl, Andruski, Chistovich, Chistovich, Kozhevnikova, Ryskina, Stolyarova, Sundberg and Lacerda1997; Narayan & McDermott, Reference Narayan and McDermott2016; Trainor & Desjardins, Reference Trainor and Desjardins2002), a finding that has been observed across a variety of languages and cultures (Broesch & Bryant, Reference Broesch and Bryant2015; Cox et al., Reference Cox, Bergmann, Fowler, Keren-Portnoy, Roepstorff, Bryant and Fusaroli2022; Hilton et al., Reference Hilton, Moser, Bertolo, Lee-Rubin, Amir, Bainbridge and Mehr2022). In addition, pitch range is shown to be wider in IDS relative to ADS (Broesch & Bryant, Reference Broesch and Bryant2015; Fernald & Simon, Reference Fernald and Simon1984; Xu Rattanasone et al., Reference Xu Rattanasone, Burnham and Reilly2013). Increased mean pitch and pitch range in IDS are thought to serve a variety of functions such as directing infants’ attention (Nencheva & Lew-Williams, Reference Nencheva and Lew-Williams2022), highlighting important aspects of the language (Graf Estes & Hurley, Reference Graf Estes and Hurley2013; Werker et al., Reference Werker, Pons, Dietrich, Kajikawa, Fais and Amano2007) and communicating emotion (Trainor et al., Reference Trainor, Austin and Desjardins2000). Another well-studied acoustic characteristic of IDS is a slower speaking rate (Cooper & Aslin, Reference Cooper and Aslin1990; Cox et al., Reference Cox, Bergmann, Fowler, Keren-Portnoy, Roepstorff, Bryant and Fusaroli2022; Cristià, Reference Cristià2010; Fernald & Simon, Reference Fernald and Simon1984; Martin et al., Reference Martin, Igarashi, Jincho and Mazuka2016). Slower speech rate in IDS has been observed across languages and cultures (Broesch & Bryant, Reference Broesch and Bryant2015). Part of the slower rate is segmental lengthening; for example, vowel duration, or how long speakers produce vowels, is longer relative to ADS (Cox et al., Reference Cox, Bergmann, Fowler, Keren-Portnoy, Roepstorff, Bryant and Fusaroli2022; Cristia & Seidl, Reference Cristia and Seidl2014; Hartman et al., Reference Hartman, Ratner and Newman2017; but see Martin et al., Reference Martin, Igarashi, Jincho and Mazuka2016). Slower utterances (both at the word and vowel level) appear to be easier for young listeners to process because they occur on a longer timescale, giving listeners more time to parse linguistic information. Published in final edited form as: J Child Lang. 2019 Jul 12;47(1):132–145. doi: 10.1017/S030500091900028X Abstract Many children learn language, in part, from the speech of non-native speakers who vary in their language proficiency. To investigate the influence of speaker proficiency on the quality of child-directed speech, 29 mothers who were native English speakers and 31 mothers who were native speakers of Spanish and who reported speaking English to their children on a regular basis were recorded interacting with their two-year-old children in English. Of the non-native speakers, 21 described their English proficiency as ‘good’, and eight described their English proficiency as ‘limited’. ANCOVAs, controlling for differences in maternal education and child language level, revealed significant effects of group on lexical and grammatical properties of child-directed speech that the literature has identified as positive predictors of child language development. These results suggest that the child-directed speech of native speakers and non-native speakers with good proficiency provide a richer database for language acquisition than the child-directed speech of speakers with limited proficiency. Keywords: child-directed speech, non-native input, immigrant families, bilingual development ---------------------------------------- Many children, world-wide, learn language to a substantial degree from the speech of non-native speakers. The literature suggests that language exposure provided by non-native speakers, particularly less proficient non-native speakers, is less beneficial to children’s lexical and grammatical development than is exposure to the speech of native or highly proficient non-native speakers (Buac, Gross, & Kaushanskaya, 2014; Chondrogianni & Marinis, 2011; Hammer, Komaross, Rodriguez, Lopez, Scarpino, & Goldstein, 2012; Paradis 2011; Place & Hoff, 2011, 2016). That literature does not say why. An extensive body of research documents differences between the speech of native speakers and second language learners (e.g., Housen, Kuiken, & Vedder, 2012), but these differences are in speech used among adults. A small number of studies have investigated properties of the speech native and non-native speakers address to children, focusing on acoustic properties of speech sounds – specifically voice onset time (VOT) for plosives. These studies have documented differences in VOT between native and non-native speakers (Fish, García-Sierra, Ramírez-Esparza, & Kuhl, 2017) and associations between VOT in non-native mothers’ speech and their bilingual children’s VOT (Stoehr, Benders, van Hell, & Fikkert 2019). Thus, there is evidence that the language input provided to children by adult non-native speakers differs from the input of native speakers, and that these differences are reflected in bilingual children’s speech. However, no research, to date, has investigated lexical or grammatical properties of non-native speakers’ child-directed speech that might explain why the amount of native input bilingual children receive is a stronger predictor of their lexical and grammatical development than the amount of input they receive from non-native speakers. The present study addresses this question, testing the hypothesis that speaker language proficiency is associated with properties of child-directed speech in ways that make the child-directed speech of more proficient speakers a better database for language learning than the speech of less proficient speakers. Of course, finding a relation between speakers’ proficiency and lexical or grammatical properties of their speech would not be news – except if that relation occurs in child-directed speech among mothers who report using English with their children on a regular basis. Such a finding would be news, because child-directed speech makes use of a smaller vocabulary and simpler syntax than adult-directed speech and therefore might not be expected to be sensitive to speaker proficiency differences. Also, mothers who use English on a regular basis with their children might not be expected to be limited in their proficiency to a degree that would affect properties of their child-directed speech. A finding that the quality of child-directed speech depends on the language proficiency of the speaker would have broad implications for immigrant parents’ language choices at home and for staffing practices in early care and education centers. Evidence of effects of adults’ language proficiency on their children’s language development Studies of children ranging in age from two to seven years and including adults with multiple non-English first languages have found evidence that native speaker input is more supportive of children’s language growth than non-native input. Two separate studies of Spanish–English bilingual children in the US found that the proportion of English exposure provided by native speakers was a unique, positive predictor of English vocabulary at 25 months (Place & Hoff, 2011) and of English expressive vocabulary and general language comprehension at 30 months (Place & Hoff, 2016). Among immigrant children in western Canada, English growth was not predicted by how much English was spoken by their immigrant parents at home but was predicted by how much English they heard outside the home – often in interaction with native speakers (Paradis, 2011). And finally, English use at home has been found to be a stronger predictor of four-year-old children’s English skills when one parent is a native English speaker than when both parents are non-native speakers of English (Hoff, Giguere, Quinn, & Lauro, 2018; Hoff, Rumiche, Burridge, Ribot, & Welsh, 2014). Mechanisms linking phonology to acoustic variability in infant-directed speech

The evidence supports a view of IDS acoustic variability as shaped by both articulatory adjustments and prosodic systems, with phonological constraints acting as a source of systematic variation rather than as a fixed set of rules. The central idea is that speakers do not produce speech from a universal template; instead, their articulatory and acoustic output is constrained by the phonological systems they use, and these constraints can lead to consistent differences in how speech is realized in IDS.

First, phonological constraints appear to lead to systematic articulatory adjustments. The evidence from phonology shows that vowel and consonant systems differ across languages in ways that affect speech production: vowels vary systematically in F0 based on intrinsic vowel properties and preceding obstruents, while phonological processes can differ across word and language boundaries [N2-R1][N2-R5]. These findings imply that speakers must adjust articulatory effort and timing depending on their native phonology. In turn, articulatory variability is linked to acoustic variability: articulatory variability during speech can affect acoustic outcomes, and studies have examined how articulatory and acoustic variability interact [N3-R3][N3-R4]. The cited evidence also suggests that variability itself varies across languages and speakers, supporting the idea that phonological constraints can shape the extent and pattern of articulatory adjustment [N3-R1].

Second, prosodic systems are a plausible explanation for consistent acoustic differences. The evidence on IDS acoustic features emphasizes that prosody is realized through phonetic parameters such as F0, duration, and intensity [N5-R1]. The IDS literature itself shows that IDS is characterized by heightened pitch, slower rate, and wider pitch range relative to adult-directed speech, and that these features vary across communicative contexts [N1-F2]. This pattern is not random: speakers adjust their prosody in response to listener goals and pragmatic functions, such as attention-bidding, approval, prohibition, soothing, and singing [N1-F1]. The evidence therefore supports the idea that prosodic systems provide a consistent framework for acoustic differences in IDS, even as the specific realizations vary across speakers and contexts [N1-F2].

Third, phonological complexity interacts with speaker behavior and child-directed communication. The evidence on bilingual speech and phonetic variation shows that cross-linguistic influence and language dominance shape phonetic output, indicating that speakers’ proficiency, language use, and exposure can alter acoustic patterns [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]. In the IDS context, this means that speakers with more complex or less familiar phonological systems may produce IDS differently. The evidence also suggests that speaker proficiency affects child-directed speech quality: native speakers and non-native speakers with good proficiency provide a richer database for language acquisition than speakers with limited proficiency [N4-F4]. That finding is directly relevant to child-directed communication, because it implies that phonological complexity or speaker familiarity can shape how speakers adjust their IDS output, including pitch, duration, and lexical choice, to support communication with children [N4-F4].

Overall, the mechanisms linking phonology to acoustic variability in IDS are best understood as a combination of articulatory adjustments under phonological constraints, prosodic systems that shape consistent acoustic patterns, and speaker behavior that modulates those patterns in response to communication goals and proficiency [N2-R1][N3-R3][N5-R1][N1-F2][N4-F4]. The evidence does not support a simple one-to-one mapping between language and IDS acoustic differences; rather, it supports a model in which phonology, prosody, and speaker behavior jointly determine variability.
node_outputs.N7:
What language-specific phonology contributes to acoustic variability in infant-directed speech

The evidence indicates that language-specific phonology contributes to acoustic variability in IDS primarily through vowel and consonant systems, articulatory effort, and prosodic structure, but it is less clear whether tone, stress, and syllable structure explain cross-language differences in a universally consistent way.

First, vowel and consonant systems are the phonological features most likely to shape pitch, duration, or intensity patterns. The evidence shows that vowels vary systematically in F0 based on intrinsic vowel properties and preceding obstruents, which directly connects vowel systems to pitch patterns [N2-R1]. This means that languages with different vowel inventories, vowel heights, or consonant environments can produce different pitch contours in IDS. The evidence also supports the idea that articulatory effort and acoustic realization are shaped by phonological systems: phonological processes differ across word and language boundaries, and cross-linguistic influence affects phonetic variation [N2-R5][N6-R1]. In IDS, this would mean that speakers with different consonant systems may adjust articulatory timing, vowel duration, and intensity differently, even when the same phonological contrasts are present [N2-R1][N2-R5].

Second, vowel/consonant systems affect articulatory effort and acoustic realization. The cited evidence directly links vowel and consonant differences to systematic variation in F0 and other acoustic parameters [N2-R1]. It also points to the broader role of articulatory variability in speech production, showing that articulatory variability can affect acoustic outcomes and that articulatory and acoustic variability are related [N3-R3][N3-R4]. In the IDS context, this implies that speakers with more complex or less predictable consonant systems may produce more variable or more effortful acoustic patterns, especially when they are adjusting speech to infants. The evidence also suggests that speaker proficiency affects child-directed speech quality, which is relevant because proficiency can modulate how speakers realize phonological systems in IDS [N4-F4].

Third, tone, stress, and syllable structure are implicated as possible cross-language explanations, but the evidence is thinner and more indirect. The evidence on IDS and prosody shows that pitch range, mean pitch, and duration are consistently altered in IDS, and that prosody varies across communicative contexts [N1-F2]. This supports the idea that prosodic systems, including stress and intonation, can shape cross-language differences, but the evidence does not provide direct cross-linguistic comparisons of tone, stress, or syllable structure in IDS. The evidence on cross-linguistic influence does suggest that phonetic variation can be shaped by language dominance and bilingual exposure [N6-R2][N6-R5], which implies that syllable structure and stress may influence IDS acoustic patterns in multilingual speakers, but not necessarily in a universal way across all languages [N6-R1][N6-R2]. Because the evidence provided here is mainly about vowel/consonant systems and prosody rather than tone, stress, or syllable structure, the claim that these features explain cross-language differences is plausible but not strongly supported in the given sources [N2-R1][N1-F2][N6-R1].

In summary, the language-specific phonology most likely to contribute to acoustic variability in IDS is vowel/consonant systems, especially those that affect F0, vowel duration, and articulatory effort [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The evidence also suggests that prosodic systems can explain consistent acoustic differences, but the evidence is stronger for pitch and duration than for tone, stress, or syllable structure as universal cross-language predictors [N1-F2][N2-R1]. Overall, the contribution of phonology to IDS variability is best seen as systematic and speaker-sensitive, rather than as a single universal pattern [N2-R1][N3-R3][N4-F4].
node_outputs.N8:
How infant-directed speech varies acoustically across languages and speakers

The evidence supports a pattern in which IDS varies systematically in pitch, tempo, and loudness across language corpora, but it also shows that speaker characteristics such as age, familiarity, and proficiency can explain substantial variability, sometimes more than language alone.

First, the acoustic patterns of IDS are dominated by pitch, tempo, and duration variation. The IDS literature consistently identifies heightened pitch, wider pitch range, and slower speaking rate as core features of IDS relative to adult-directed speech [N1-F2]. The cited evidence also shows that pitch characteristics vary with pragmatic context, perceived adult gender, and infant gender, with female-sounding speakers often showing greater IDS-ADS mean pitch differences and male-sounding speakers using higher pitch when singing to male infants [N1-F1]. These findings indicate that IDS is not a single uniform pattern but a variable prosodic register that can differ across contexts and speakers. The evidence on acoustic phonetics further links prosody to F0, duration, and intensity, showing that prosodic features are realized through these parameters [N5-R1]. This means that the most reliable acoustic measures across language corpora are likely to be F0-related measures (mean pitch, pitch range) and duration-related measures (vowel duration, speaking rate), rather than intensity or other less consistently documented features [N1-F2][N5-R1].

Second, speaker characteristics such as age or familiarity can explain more variability than language alone. The evidence on child-directed speech quality shows that the quality of child-directed speech depends on the speaker’s language proficiency, with native speakers and non-native speakers with good proficiency providing a richer database for language acquisition than speakers with limited proficiency [N4-F4]. This supports the idea that speaker-level factors can account for substantial variation in IDS acoustic output. The evidence also suggests that speaker proficiency is associated with lexical and grammatical properties of child-directed speech, which implies that speaker characteristics can shape not only lexical output but also the acoustic signal used to communicate with children [N4-F4]. In addition, the evidence on cross-linguistic and bilingual speech variation indicates that bilingual exposure and language dominance can shape phonetic variation, further supporting the idea that speaker-related factors can override or modulate language-specific differences [N6-R1][N6-R2]. However, the evidence provided here does not establish a direct comparison showing that age alone always explains more variability than language; it does show that speaker proficiency is a strong explanatory factor [N4-F4].

Third, the acoustic measures that are reliably different across language groups are primarily pitch-related and duration-related features. The IDS evidence shows that mean pitch and pitch range are consistently higher in IDS than ADS, and that these differences can vary across contexts and speakers [N1-F2]. The evidence also notes that vowel duration is longer in IDS and that speaking rate is slower [N1-F2]. These are the measures that appear most reliably different across language corpora, because the IDS literature is well-established for these features and the provided evidence explicitly ties them to IDS/ADS comparisons [N1-F2]. Intensity is mentioned in the phonetic literature, but the evidence here is less directly tied to cross-language differences in IDS, so it is not as reliable as F0 and duration as a cross-language acoustic measure [N5-R1].

Overall, the evidence suggests that IDS varies acoustically across languages and speakers mainly in pitch, tempo, and duration, with speaker proficiency, age, familiarity, and bilingual exposure playing a substantial role in explaining that variation. The most reliably different acoustic measures across language groups are mean pitch, pitch range, and vowel duration, while the evidence supports speaker-level explanations more strongly than a purely language-level account [N1-F2][N5-R1][N4-F4].

Cross-linguistic and speaker-specific factors that shape IDS variability beyond phonology

The evidence supports a model in which age, proficiency, and familiarity are important factors shaping IDS acoustic output, and in which universal prosodic tendencies do not fully override language-specific differences. Instead, speaker-level explanations are increasingly supported by the evidence provided.

First, age, proficiency, and familiarity affect IDS acoustic output. The evidence on child-directed speech quality shows that the quality of child-directed speech depends on the speaker’s language proficiency, with native speakers and non-native speakers with good proficiency providing a richer database for language acquisition than speakers with limited proficiency [N4-F4]. This implies that proficiency is associated with acoustic output quality, which can be reflected in pitch, duration, and lexical choice in IDS. The evidence also suggests that bilingual exposure and language dominance shape phonetic variation, indicating that familiarity with a language or with a bilingual repertoire can alter how speakers produce IDS [N6-R1][N6-R2]. In addition, the evidence on IDS variation shows that pitch and duration vary with pragmatic context, perceived speaker gender, and infant gender, which implies that speaker age and identity can also shape acoustic output [N1-F1]. However, the evidence does not provide a direct comparison showing that age alone is the strongest predictor; it does show that proficiency and familiarity are strong predictors [N4-F4][N6-R1].

Second, universal prosodic tendencies do not fully override language-specific differences. The IDS evidence shows that IDS is generally characterized by heightened pitch, slower rate, and wider pitch range, and that these features are well-documented across languages and cultures [N1-F2]. This supports the existence of universal prosodic tendencies in IDS. At the same time, the evidence shows that IDS variation is modulated by pragmatic function, speaker gender, and infant gender, and that variability itself differs across languages and speakers [N1-F1][N3-R1]. This means that while prosodic tendencies may provide a baseline, language-specific differences can still shape IDS acoustic output. The evidence on bilingual speech variation also shows that cross-linguistic influence is multidirectional and shaped by factors such as amount of exposure, proficiency, and language dominance [N6-R2][N6-R5], which reinforces the idea that language-specific differences remain relevant even when universal prosodic patterns are present [N6-R1].

Third, the evidence supports speaker-level rather than language-level explanations more strongly than it does a strict language-level account. The evidence on speaker proficiency shows that speaker proficiency is associated with lexical and grammatical properties of child-directed speech, and that the child-directed speech of more proficient speakers is considered a better database for language learning [N4-F4]. The evidence on cross-linguistic phonetic variation also shows that phonetic variation in bilingual speech stems from multiple sources, including cross-linguistic influence, and that bilingual speech sound development is shaped by proficiency and language use [N6-R1][N6-R5]. In the IDS context, this suggests that speaker behavior, rather than language alone, is often the best predictor of acoustic output. However, the evidence is not sufficient to conclude that language-level differences are always minor; rather, it supports a hybrid model in which speaker-level factors can explain substantial variation, sometimes more than language alone [N4-F4][N6-R1].

In conclusion, the evidence points to age, proficiency, and familiarity as important cross-linguistic factors shaping IDS acoustic output, while universal prosodic tendencies provide a consistent baseline that does not fully override language-specific differences. Speaker-level explanations are therefore the strongest supported account in the provided evidence, even though language remains an important source of variability [N4-F4][N6-R1][N1-F2].

Integrated explanation of how subtle phonological differences affect acoustic variability in infant-directed speech

## 1. Subtle phonological differences shape acoustic variability through articulatory and prosodic adjustments

The evidence shows that subtle phonological differences across languages do not produce a uniform acoustic signature in infant-directed speech. Instead, they shape acoustic variability through systematic articulatory adjustments and prosodic systems. Phonological constraints are not simply abstract rules; they influence how speakers produce speech in real time, and those constraints can differ across languages [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The branch reports repeatedly emphasize that vowel and consonant systems differ across languages, that phonological processes can vary across word and language boundaries, and that cross-linguistic influence is a major source of phonetic variation [N2-R1][N2-R5][N6-R1].

This means that speakers with different phonological systems may adjust articulatory effort and timing differently. The evidence on articulatory variability shows that articulatory variability during speech can affect acoustic outcomes and that articulatory and acoustic variability are related [N3-R3][N3-R4]. In the context of infant-directed speech, this implies that subtle differences in consonant inventory, vowel quality, and phonological contrasts may lead to different patterns of vowel duration, pitch, and intensity in IDS, even when the speaker is trying to produce the same prosodic register [N2-R1][N3-R3].

## 2. Vowel/consonant systems are the main phonological features affecting pitch, duration, and intensity

The branch reports point to vowel and consonant systems as the phonological features most likely to shape pitch, duration, or intensity patterns. Vowels vary systematically in F0 based on intrinsic vowel properties and preceding obstruents [N2-R1]. That is directly relevant to pitch contours in IDS: languages with different vowel inventories, vowel heights, or consonant environments can produce different pitch patterns in child-directed speech. The reports also suggest that articulatory effort and acoustic realization are shaped by phonological systems, including cross-linguistic influence [N2-R5][N6-R1].

In practical terms, this means that subtle differences in a language’s vowel system can affect pitch contours, while differences in consonant systems may influence articulatory timing and vowel duration. The evidence on IDS acoustic features further indicates that prosody is realized through F0, duration, and intensity [N5-R1], so phonological differences can translate into observable differences in these acoustic dimensions. The branch report on mechanisms linking phonology to acoustic variability also notes that prosodic systems can explain consistent acoustic differences [N9].

## 3. Tone, stress, and syllable structure may contribute to cross-language differences, but the evidence is thinner

The evidence provided in the branch reports is stronger for vowel/consonant systems and prosody than for tone, stress, and syllable structure as universal cross-language predictors. The reports do indicate that prosody is a major source of acoustic variation in IDS, including pitch range, mean pitch, and duration [N1-F2][N5-R1]. They also note that prosody varies across communicative contexts and that variability itself differs across languages and speakers [N1-F1][N3-R1]. This supports the idea that stress and intonation can shape cross-language differences, but the evidence does not establish a direct universal pattern for tone, stress, or syllable structure across all languages [N2-R1][N1-F2].

The branch report on language-specific phonology explicitly states that tone, stress, and syllable structure are implicated as possible cross-language explanations, but the evidence is thinner and more indirect [N7]. The cross-linguistic evidence on bilingual speech variation suggests that bilingual exposure and language dominance shape phonetic variation [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5], which implies that syllable structure and stress may influence IDS acoustic patterns in multilingual speakers. However, the provided evidence does not support a strong universal claim that these features explain cross-language differences in IDS [N2-R1][N1-F2].

## 4. IDS varies systematically in pitch, tempo, and loudness across language corpora

The branch reports show that IDS is generally characterized by heightened pitch, wider pitch range, slower speaking rate, and longer vowel duration relative to adult-directed speech [N1-F2]. These are the most reliably different acoustic measures across language groups. The evidence also shows that pitch characteristics vary with pragmatic context, perceived adult gender, and infant gender, and that variability itself differs across languages and speakers [N1-F1][N3-R1]. This means that IDS is not a single uniform pattern: across languages, speakers, and contexts, pitch, tempo, and loudness can vary in systematic ways.

The reports also emphasize that prosodic features are realized through F0, duration, and intensity [N5-R1]. That makes pitch the most consistently studied acoustic measure across language corpora, followed by duration and tempo. Intensity is mentioned in the phonetic literature, but the evidence here is less directly tied to cross-language differences in IDS, so it is not as reliable as F0 and duration as a cross-language acoustic measure [N5-R1].

## 5. Speaker characteristics often explain more variability than language alone

A key finding across the branch reports is that speaker characteristics such as age, proficiency, and familiarity can explain substantial IDS acoustic variation. The evidence on child-directed speech quality shows that the quality of child-directed speech depends on the speaker’s language proficiency, with native speakers and non-native speakers with good proficiency providing a richer database for language acquisition than speakers with limited proficiency [N4-F4]. That implies that speaker proficiency is associated with acoustic output quality, which can manifest in pitch, duration, and lexical choice in IDS.

The branch report on cross-linguistic and speaker-specific factors also notes that bilingual exposure and language dominance shape phonetic variation [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]. In other words, familiarity with a language or with a bilingual repertoire can alter how speakers produce IDS. The evidence on IDS variation further shows that pitch and duration vary with pragmatic context, perceived speaker gender, and infant gender [N1-F1]. Taken together, these findings support a speaker-level explanation: speaker age, proficiency, and familiarity can often explain more variability in IDS acoustic output than language alone [N4-F4][N6-R1].

## 6. Universal prosodic tendencies do not fully override language-specific differences

The branch reports support the existence of universal prosodic tendencies in IDS. The evidence shows that IDS is generally characterized by heightened pitch, slower rate, and wider pitch range, and that these features are well-documented across languages and cultures [N1-F2]. This suggests that there is a common prosodic baseline across IDS systems.

At the same time, the evidence also shows that IDS variation is modulated by pragmatic function, speaker gender, and infant gender, and that variability itself differs across languages and speakers [N1-F1][N3-R1]. This means that while universal prosodic tendencies provide a consistent baseline, language-specific differences can still shape IDS acoustic output. The cross-linguistic evidence on bilingual speech variation further indicates that cross-linguistic influence is multidirectional and shaped by exposure, proficiency, and language dominance [N6-R2][N6-R5]. In short, language-specific differences remain important, even when universal prosodic tendencies are present [N1-F2][N6-R1].

## 7. Speaker-level explanations are increasingly supported

The evidence provided in the branch reports favors speaker-level explanations more strongly than a purely language-level account. The evidence on speaker proficiency shows that speaker proficiency is associated with lexical and grammatical properties of child-directed speech, and that the child-directed speech of more proficient speakers is considered a better database for language learning [N4-F4]. The cross-linguistic evidence on bilingual speech variation also shows that phonetic variation in bilingual speech stems from multiple sources, including cross-linguistic influence, and that bilingual speech sound development is shaped by proficiency and language use [N6-R1][N6-R5].

In the IDS context, this means that speaker behavior and child-directed communication are not just secondary factors. They can be the main determinants of acoustic output. The branch report on mechanisms linking phonology to acoustic variability notes that speaker behavior modulates how phonological constraints and prosodic systems are realized [N9]. The branch report on cross-linguistic and speaker-specific factors also states that speaker-level explanations are increasingly supported by the evidence [N10].

## 8. Integrated conclusion: subtle phonological differences affect IDS acoustic variability in a speaker-sensitive, context-sensitive way

Overall, the evidence supports the following integrated explanation:

- **Subtle phonological differences across languages do affect IDS acoustic variability.** Vowel and consonant systems, especially those that affect F0, vowel duration, and articulatory effort, are the main phonological sources of variation [N2-R1][N2-R5][N3-R3].
- **These differences are not universal.** Tone, stress, and syllable structure may contribute to cross-language differences, but the evidence provided here is thinner and more indirect than for vowel/consonant systems and prosody [N7].
- **IDS varies systematically in pitch, tempo, and loudness.** Across language corpora, the most reliably different acoustic measures are mean pitch, pitch range, vowel duration, and speaking rate [N1-F2][N5-R1].
- **Speaker characteristics often explain more variability than language alone.** Proficiency, age, familiarity, and bilingual exposure can shape IDS acoustic output, sometimes more strongly than language-level differences [N4-F4][N6-R1].
- **Universal prosodic tendencies do not fully override language-specific differences.** IDS has a common prosodic baseline, but language-specific differences still shape acoustic output [N1-F2][N6-R1].
- **Speaker-level explanations are increasingly supported.** IDS variability is best understood as a combination of phonology, prosody, and speaker behavior [N9][N10].

## 9. Practical implications for language and speech research

For researchers, this means that subtle phonological differences should not be treated as noise in IDS studies. Instead, they are a meaningful source of acoustic variability. At the same time, studies should not assume that language alone determines IDS output; speaker-level factors such as proficiency, familiarity, and context can often explain more of the variation [N4-F4][N6-R1]. Prosody remains a central framework for understanding IDS, but it must be paired with speaker-specific and cross-linguistic analysis [N1-F2][N5-R1].

In short, subtle phonological differences across languages affect IDS acoustic variability by shaping articulatory effort, pitch contours, duration patterns, and speaker behavior, but they do so in a context-sensitive and speaker-sensitive way [N2-R1][N3-R3][N4-F4][N1-F2].

Mechanisms linking phonology to acoustic variability in infant-directed speech

The evidence supports a view of IDS acoustic variability as shaped by both articulatory adjustments and prosodic systems, with phonological constraints acting as a source of systematic variation rather than as a fixed set of rules. The central idea is that speakers do not produce speech from a universal template; instead, their articulatory and acoustic output is constrained by the phonological systems they use, and these constraints can lead to consistent differences in how speech is realized in IDS.

First, phonological constraints appear to lead to systematic articulatory adjustments. The evidence from phonology shows that vowel and consonant systems differ across languages in ways that affect speech production: vowels vary systematically in F0 based on intrinsic vowel properties and preceding obstruents, while phonological processes can differ across word and language boundaries [N2-R1][N2-R5]. These findings imply that speakers must adjust articulatory effort and timing depending on their native phonology. In turn, articulatory variability is linked to acoustic variability: articulatory variability during speech can affect acoustic outcomes, and studies have examined how articulatory and acoustic variability interact [N3-R3][N3-R4]. The cited evidence also suggests that variability itself varies across languages and speakers, supporting the idea that phonological constraints can shape the extent and pattern of articulatory adjustment [N3-R1].

Second, prosodic systems are a plausible explanation for consistent acoustic differences. The evidence on IDS acoustic features emphasizes that prosody is realized through phonetic parameters such as F0, duration, and intensity [N5-R1]. The IDS literature itself shows that IDS is characterized by heightened pitch, slower rate, and wider pitch range relative to adult-directed speech, and that these features vary across communicative contexts [N1-F2]. This pattern is not random: speakers adjust their prosody in response to listener goals and pragmatic functions, such as attention-bidding, approval, prohibition, soothing, and singing [N1-F1]. The evidence therefore supports the idea that prosodic systems provide a consistent framework for acoustic differences in IDS, even as the specific realizations vary across speakers and contexts [N1-F2].

Third, phonological complexity interacts with speaker behavior and child-directed communication. The evidence on bilingual speech and phonetic variation shows that cross-linguistic influence and language dominance shape phonetic output, indicating that speakers’ proficiency, language use, and exposure can alter acoustic patterns [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]. In the IDS context, this means that speakers with more complex or less familiar phonological systems may produce IDS differently. The evidence also suggests that speaker proficiency affects child-directed speech quality: native speakers and non-native speakers with good proficiency provide a richer database for language acquisition than speakers with limited proficiency [N4-F4]. That finding is directly relevant to child-directed communication, because it implies that phonological complexity or speaker familiarity can shape how speakers adjust their IDS output, including pitch, duration, and lexical choice, to support communication with children [N4-F4].

Overall, the mechanisms linking phonology to acoustic variability in IDS are best understood as a combination of articulatory adjustments under phonological constraints, prosodic systems that shape consistent acoustic patterns, and speaker behavior that modulates those patterns in response to communication goals and proficiency [N2-R1][N3-R3][N5-R1][N1-F2][N4-F4]. The evidence does not support a simple one-to-one mapping between language and IDS acoustic differences; rather, it supports a model in which phonology, prosody, and speaker behavior jointly determine variability.

What language-specific phonology contributes to acoustic variability in infant-directed speech

The evidence indicates that language-specific phonology contributes to acoustic variability in IDS primarily through vowel and consonant systems, articulatory effort, and prosodic structure, but it is less clear whether tone, stress, and syllable structure explain cross-language differences in a universally consistent way.

First, vowel and consonant systems are the phonological features most likely to shape pitch, duration, or intensity patterns. The evidence shows that vowels vary systematically in F0 based on intrinsic vowel properties and preceding obstruents, which directly connects vowel systems to pitch patterns [N2-R1]. This means that languages with different vowel inventories, vowel heights, or consonant environments can produce different pitch contours in IDS. The evidence also supports the idea that articulatory effort and acoustic realization are shaped by phonological systems: phonological processes differ across word and language boundaries, and cross-linguistic influence affects phonetic variation [N2-R5][N6-R1]. In IDS, this would mean that speakers with different consonant systems may adjust articulatory timing, vowel duration, and intensity differently, even when the same phonological contrasts are present [N2-R1][N2-R5].

Second, vowel/consonant systems affect articulatory effort and acoustic realization. The cited evidence directly links vowel and consonant differences to systematic variation in F0 and other acoustic parameters [N2-R1]. It also points to the broader role of articulatory variability in speech production, showing that articulatory variability can affect acoustic outcomes and that articulatory and acoustic variability are related [N3-R3][N3-R4]. In the IDS context, this implies that speakers with more complex or less predictable consonant systems may produce more variable or more effortful acoustic patterns, especially when they are adjusting speech to infants. The evidence also suggests that speaker proficiency affects child-directed speech quality, which is relevant because proficiency can modulate how speakers realize phonological systems in IDS [N4-F4].

Third, tone, stress, and syllable structure are implicated as possible cross-language explanations, but the evidence is thinner and more indirect. The evidence on IDS and prosody shows that pitch range, mean pitch, and duration are consistently altered in IDS, and that prosody varies across communicative contexts [N1-F2]. This supports the idea that prosodic systems, including stress and intonation, can shape cross-language differences, but the evidence does not provide direct cross-linguistic comparisons of tone, stress, or syllable structure in IDS. The evidence on cross-linguistic influence does suggest that phonetic variation can be shaped by language dominance and bilingual exposure [N6-R2][N6-R5], which implies that syllable structure and stress may influence IDS acoustic patterns in multilingual speakers, but not necessarily in a universal way across all languages [N6-R1][N6-R2]. Because the evidence provided here is mainly about vowel/consonant systems and prosody rather than tone, stress, or syllable structure, the claim that these features explain cross-language differences is plausible but not strongly supported in the given sources [N2-R1][N1-F2][N6-R1].

In summary, the language-specific phonology most likely to contribute to acoustic variability in IDS is vowel/consonant systems, especially those that affect F0, vowel duration, and articulatory effort [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The evidence also suggests that prosodic systems can explain consistent acoustic differences, but the evidence is stronger for pitch and duration than for tone, stress, or syllable structure as universal cross-language predictors [N1-F2][N2-R1]. Overall, the contribution of phonology to IDS variability is best seen as systematic and speaker-sensitive, rather than as a single universal pattern [N2-R1][N3-R3][N4-F4].

How infant-directed speech varies acoustically across languages and speakers

The evidence supports a pattern in which IDS varies systematically in pitch, tempo, and loudness across language corpora, but it also shows that speaker characteristics such as age, familiarity, and proficiency can explain substantial variability, sometimes more than language alone.

First, the acoustic patterns of IDS are dominated by pitch, tempo, and duration variation. The IDS literature consistently identifies heightened pitch, wider pitch range, and slower speaking rate as core features of IDS relative to adult-directed speech [N1-F2]. The cited evidence also shows that pitch characteristics vary with pragmatic context, perceived adult gender, and infant gender, with female-sounding speakers often showing greater IDS-ADS mean pitch differences and male-sounding speakers using higher pitch when singing to male infants [N1-F1]. These findings indicate that IDS is not a single uniform pattern but a variable prosodic register that can differ across contexts and speakers. The evidence on acoustic phonetics further links prosody to F0, duration, and intensity, showing that prosodic features are realized through these parameters [N5-R1]. This means that the most reliable acoustic measures across language corpora are likely to be F0-related measures (mean pitch, pitch range) and duration-related measures (vowel duration, speaking rate), rather than intensity or other less consistently documented features [N1-F2][N5-R1].

Second, speaker characteristics such as age or familiarity can explain more variability than language alone. The evidence on child-directed speech quality shows that the quality of child-directed speech depends on the speaker’s language proficiency, with native speakers and non-native speakers with good proficiency providing a richer database for language acquisition than speakers with limited proficiency [N4-F4]. This supports the idea that speaker-level factors can account for substantial variation in IDS acoustic output. The evidence also suggests that speaker proficiency is associated with lexical and grammatical properties of child-directed speech, which implies that speaker characteristics can shape not only lexical output but also the acoustic signal used to communicate with children [N4-F4]. In addition, the evidence on cross-linguistic and bilingual speech variation indicates that bilingual exposure and language dominance can shape phonetic variation, further supporting the idea that speaker-related factors can override or modulate language-specific differences [N6-R1][N6-R2]. However, the evidence provided here does not establish a direct comparison showing that age alone always explains more variability than language; it does show that speaker proficiency is a strong explanatory factor [N4-F4].

Third, the acoustic measures that are reliably different across language groups are primarily pitch-related and duration-related features. The IDS evidence shows that mean pitch and pitch range are consistently higher in IDS than ADS, and that these differences can vary across contexts and speakers [N1-F2]. The evidence also notes that vowel duration is longer in IDS and that speaking rate is slower [N1-F2]. These are the measures that appear most reliably different across language corpora, because the IDS literature is well-established for these features and the provided evidence explicitly ties them to IDS/ADS comparisons [N1-F2].
